passage: You're fifteen and worried about a friend who has gone quiet? Then listen, because I had that too. I'm Chetan, and my best friend Leela stopped answering me one October. No fight, no reason. For nights I replayed every word I'd said: the joke at the bus stop, the time I forgot her birthday by a day. I felt I must be the problem. Then my uncle said, "Write to her once and say it plainly. After that, let it be." So I wrote, "I miss talking to you. If I did something, tell me. If you need space, that's okay." I sent it once. No reply came. It was hard, but I put the phone in the drawer and went to play cricket. I never found out why. But I stopped blaming myself, and one day the silence just felt like hers, not mine.

qa.q: What did Chetan's uncle advise about Leela's silence?
qa.a: He told Chetan to write to Leela once, say it plainly, and after that let it be.

qa.q: How did Chetan feel during those nights of silence?
qa.a: Chetan felt anxious and to blame, replaying every word said to Leela, like the joke at the bus stop and the forgotten birthday.

qa.q: What helped Chetan stop chasing the answer?
qa.a: Chetan sent one honest message, then put the phone in the drawer and went to play cricket, accepting the silence instead of messaging again.

qa.q: How might Leela's silence have looked from her side?
qa.a: We cannot tell. She may have had her own reasons for pulling away that had nothing to do with anything Chetan said, which is why Chetan stopped taking the blame.

grounding: Chetan's close friend stopped replying without a reason, and after replaying everything Chetan sent one honest message and then accepted the silence.

passage: I sit behind Hrithik in class, so I saw the whole thing. For about two months he and Pankaj talked every single day, and Hrithik would grin at his phone under the desk. Then Pankaj just stopped. No fight that I know of. Hrithik still kept the phone face up, checking it in every break. He looked pale. At lunch he said, "It's like I was never there," and then went quiet. His cousin told him to make a fake account to see Pankaj's page. Hrithik laughed and said no, that would be weird. Four of us have taken him to the ground since. I can't say what's really in his head, but he seems to be grieving something. I just know he's not sitting alone.

qa.q: For how long did Hrithik and Pankaj talk every day before it stopped?
qa.a: They talked every single day for about two months.

qa.q: What might Hrithik be feeling, and what makes the classmate say so?
qa.a: He may be hurt and grieving. He keeps the phone face up, looks pale, and says, "It's like I was never there," though the classmate admits they cannot be sure what is in his head.

qa.q: What did Hrithik and his friends do that was healthy?
qa.a: Hrithik refused his cousin's idea of a fake account, and his classmates took him to the ground so he has company.

qa.q: How might Pankaj's silence look from Hrithik's side?
qa.a: It feels like erasure, as if the daily talks did not count. The silence probably says more about Pankaj avoiding than about Hrithik's worth.

grounding: After daily talks a crush vanished on Hrithik, seen by a classmate, who notes his hurt, his refusal of a fake account and his friends' company.

passage:
Day 1. Zainab read Aditi's message, "Are you free after school?", and put her phone in her bag. She didn't want to hurt Aditi, but she'd been feeling suffocated lately, and she didn't know how to say she needed some space. So she said nothing.

Day 4. Aditi wrote, "Did I do something?" Zainab's stomach twisted. She walked to class a different way to avoid Aditi's corridor. Her chest felt tight every time the phone buzzed, and she felt like a coward.

Day 9. She finally typed, "I'm sorry I went silent. I need some space right now. It's not about anything you did." Sent. Aditi replied an hour later: "Thanks for telling me. It hurts, but I'd rather know." Zainab breathed out slowly.

qa.q: What did Zainab do when Aditi asked if she was free after school on Day 1?
qa.a: She read the message and put her phone in her bag, saying nothing.

qa.q: Why did Zainab avoid replying at first?
qa.a: She wanted distance but did not know how to say it and did not want to hurt Aditi, so she stayed silent. She also felt like a coward.

qa.q: What did Zainab do on Day 9 that was kinder than silence?
qa.a: She sent a short honest message saying she needed space and that it was not about anything Aditi did.

qa.q: How might Aditi have felt during the days of silence?
qa.a: Confused and worried, since Aditi asked, "Did I do something?" Afterwards Aditi said it hurt but was better than not knowing.

grounding: Zainab avoided replying because she did not know how to ask for distance, then sent a short honest message.

passage: I had five replies drafted, each meaner than the last. I'm Arohi, and that Monday I found out Kamal had walked to the canteen with the new group and never told me, and hadn't answered my messages for a week. My face was hot for hours. In the notes on my phone I wrote things like "Guess I was only useful for your maths notes." I read them out loud to myself in the bathroom mirror and felt powerful for maybe a minute. Then my mother called me for dinner and I realised I was shaking. I didn't send any of them. I slept badly, and by Thursday the anger had gone quieter. I asked myself if Kamal was worth one calm message. I wrote, "I noticed you've been distant. If something's up, tell me." Then I put the phone away.

qa.q: Where did Arohi write the cutting replies?
qa.a: In the notes on Arohi's phone.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling on Monday, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Furious and hurt. Arohi's face was hot for hours, the mean replies got read aloud in the mirror, and by dinner Arohi was shaking.

qa.q: What did Arohi do to keep some dignity?
qa.a: Arohi did not send the drafts, let the anger settle for a few days, and then sent one calm message before putting the phone away.

qa.q: How might Kamal see Arohi's final message?
qa.a: Perhaps as a surprise, since it is calm and not blaming. It gives Kamal an easy way to explain if Kamal wants to.

grounding: Arohi is furious at being dropped and rehearses cutting replies, then lets the anger cool and sends one calm message.

passage: The school canteen was so loud that Pema had to lean across the table, and there were only fifteen minutes before the bell. Varun was three chairs down, laughing with the new footballers, his back half turned to her. It had been like that since summer. She'd sat next to him every lunch for two years, and now she was somebody he waved at. Her throat tightened. She waited until he stood to throw away his wrapper, and caught him by the bin. "I feel like background lately," she said. "I just wanted to say it once." Varun blinked. "Oh. I didn't mean that. Sorry." But the bell rang and he was already swept off by the team. Pema stood there, hurt, then walked toward the photography club table, where Dolma looked up and moved her bag off the chair.

qa.q: How long did Pema have before the bell?
qa.a: She had only fifteen minutes.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling as she watched Varun with the footballers?
qa.a: Hurt and left out. Her throat tightened when she thought about him treating her as somebody he only waved at.

qa.q: What did Pema do that was wise?
qa.a: She named the problem to Varun once, then turned toward the photography club, where Dolma made room, investing in a new friendship.

qa.q: How might Varun have seen it?
qa.a: Surprised and a little guilty, since he says he didn't mean that. He is busy with the team and probably did not notice how it felt for Pema.

grounding: Pema's best friend has moved on to new people and treats her as background; she names it once and invests in new, reciprocal friendships.

passage: It felt like I was a hobby he picked up when he was bored. I'm Dhruv, and with Manoj it went like this: I'd text at lunch and he'd reply at eleven at night with "hey." When he wanted something, like help with his physics, he was instantly warm. Two days of nothing, then a joke, and I'd say, "No worries!" while my chest felt small. I kept calling it patience. Eventually I told him, "I need you to reply during the day when I write about something that matters to me." He said, "Sure, sorry," and for three days it was better. Then it was back. So I stepped back. I stopped waiting by the phone and started playing football again. It felt like standing on cold ground, but I'd rather be lonely than be ignored while pretending it's fine.

qa.q: When would Manoj usually reply to Dhruv's lunchtime texts?
qa.a: He would reply at eleven at night with "hey."

qa.q: Why did Dhruv keep saying "No worries!" while feeling small inside?
qa.a: Dhruv was calling the waiting patience, when really Dhruv was lowering standards and feeling hurt inside.

qa.q: What did Dhruv do when Manoj's replies stayed the same?
qa.a: Dhruv told Manoj what was needed, and when it did not change, stepped back and went back to playing football.

qa.q: How might Manoj see the situation?
qa.a: He may believe that saying sorry is enough, since things improved for three days, without seeing how much it matters to Dhruv to hear back.

grounding: Manoj answers Dhruv only when convenient, so Dhruv says what is needed and, when nothing changes, steps back.

passage: I'm Parul, and I was in that chat, so I watched Vasudha. Someone posted a picture of Ananya's haircut, and the jokes started: one, then five, then ten laughing faces. Vasudha typed "lol she looks like a mop" almost straight away, faster than anyone. She's usually kind. In the corridor afterwards, she kept checking the chat, her smile stuck on her face. When Ananya walked by with her head down, Vasudha stared at the floor. I can't be certain, but she looked like she wanted to disappear. That evening I saw her typing for a long time in a private window with Ananya. Ananya later told me it said, "That was unkind. I'm sorry I joined in." I can't tell if Vasudha was scared of being next, but I think she was.

qa.q: What was the picture someone posted in the chat?
qa.a: It was a picture of Ananya's haircut.

qa.q: What might Vasudha have been feeling in the corridor, according to Parul?
qa.a: Uneasy and perhaps ashamed. She kept checking the chat with a stuck smile and stared at the floor when Ananya passed, though Parul is not sure.

qa.q: What did Vasudha do afterwards that helped?
qa.a: She sent Ananya a private message saying it was unkind and that she was sorry for joining in.

qa.q: How might Ananya have felt seeing the chat and then reading Vasudha's message?
qa.a: Hurt by the mocking and head-down in the corridor, and then perhaps somewhat comforted, at least, by a private apology.

grounding: Vasudha joins mocking a classmate in a group chat because everyone is laughing, and later sends the classmate a kind private message; a peer observes her.

passage: I'm Shankar, and last term I was admin of our class chat. It gave me a little tap-and-they're-gone power over everyone, and I liked that. One night Lokesh sent a long, boring voice note about cricket stats, and three loud boys wrote, "Remove him lol." My finger was already on his name. It would have been easy, and they'd have cheered for me. But I saw that they wanted a show, and that Lokesh would see the notification alone in his room. It made my stomach tight. I didn't remove him. I posted, "Voice notes under a minute please, everyone," and made the rule for everyone. The loud boys grumbled for a day. Lokesh sent me a thumbs up. I've thought since about how nice it felt to hold that button, and how quickly I could have used it to hurt someone.

qa.q: What kind of message did Lokesh send that night?
qa.a: He sent a long voice note about cricket stats.

qa.q: What was Shankar thinking with a finger already on Lokesh's name?
qa.a: Shankar knew it would be easy and the loud boys would cheer, but saw that they wanted a show and that Lokesh would see it alone. The tight stomach shows unease.

qa.q: What could Shankar do in future to use admin power fairly?
qa.a: Shankar can keep making rules that apply to everybody, like the one-minute voice note limit, and never remove anyone just to please the loud ones.

qa.q: How might Lokesh have felt if Shankar had removed him?
qa.a: Humiliated and alone. Getting a thumbs-up instead suggests he felt relieved and respected.

grounding: Shankar enjoys the control of being group admin but uses it fairly instead of removing someone to please the loud ones.
